Some thoughts on my first project, a box, and its ultimate destruction

A sand paper holder sounds like a good little project.

I generally stick to hand tools with my wood working (I don't have a table saw, but it sure would be handy) and I make boxes to put my tools in as practice. I make mine out of scrap pallet wood that I need to dress and dimension with hand planes first. It's good practice.

You said your box fell apart when it was dropped. What sort of joinery did you use for the corners? Since you have a table saw, you could do a box joint pretty easily that should be really strong. I tend to go with fairly dodgy hand cut dove tails, as long as they're reasonably tight I generally don't need glue.

Definitely get a hand plane (don't bother with an electric one, just get a second hand one and clean it up). For a first plane, I'd probably go with a #5. They're a little longer than an #4 and can be used for flattening a reasonably large surface quite well. Things to look for are:

  • Quality body (Stanley or Record are good makers), avoid cheap new knock offs, the quality of the castings and mechanism is often terrible. There should ideally be a brass blade adjustment knob and a screw at the back of the frog for moving the frog forward and backward (cheaper planes may not have this). The surfaces that the frog rests on should be flat machined surfaces. I've seen cheap planes where the mating surface between the frog and the body was just the rough casting (smoothed out with paint).
  • No cracks (particularly around the mouth).
  • Not too much pitting on the bottom. If you buy second hand, it'll likely have a bit of rust, but watch out for heavy pitting, particularly on the sole. Generally, I flatten the bottom of any plane I get (they're never flat) anyway, which can be done by lapping on progressively finer grades of sand paper stuck to a flat surface (plate glass is good for this).

Here's a good guide to restoring a second hand bench plane if you get one: https://paulsellers.com/2016/01/restoring-bench-plane-video-on-youtube/

You'll need more clamps.

I generally stick to hand tools with my wood working

Welcome to the typical project progression...at least for me!

Some advice on cutting to size; rough cut all your pieces to within 1” of your end measurements and “walk” your cuts down one kerf at a time until it fits in place. To do it best you’ll need a crosscut sled for your table saw but a miter saw will work if your not up for making one yet. I cut the bottom panel for a toy box like this this morning. It fit snuggly into the rabbet I’d dado’d into the bottom too. Rough cut. Try the fit. Cut another thin kerf. Try to fit again. Repeat until fits.

Hand planes are a bit above your pay grade like now. Don’t get me wrong. Buy a couple. Plane away on some scrap. But it’s going to be a while before you’re gonna want to take that plane to some $18 a board foot material. Cabinet scrapers though. Those are achievable for a novice.

Titebond III is some strong glue. Either you didn’t use enough or the wood you were working on was still wet. Wasn’t pressure treated pine was it?
